item.title: BAIT: Large Language Model Backdoor Scanning by Inverting Attack Target
item.description:
The paper “BAIT: Large Language Model Backdoor Scanning by Inverting Attack Target” addresses backdoor (trojan) attacks in LLMs by proactively detecting hidden triggers through attack target inversion.

Core Innovation

  • Backdoor detection via inversion: Instead of waiting for malicious prompts, BAIT reconstructs potential trojan triggers to expose hidden vulnerabilities.
  • Non-intrusive scanning: Works without retraining, allowing safe inspection of deployed models.

Architectural Highlights

  • Scans models across layers to detect vulnerabilities.
  • Works efficiently on models up to 13B parameters, demonstrating scalability to large LLMs.

Comparison & Key Insights

  • Detection accuracy: BAIT achieves ~90%, outperforming prior methods:
    • STRIP: ~70%
    • Standard anomaly detection: ~65%
  • Backdoors can exist even in models that appear safe.
  • Inverting the attack target is a more systematic and reliable approach than previous defenses.

📄 Read the paper for full details and experiments:
BAIT

item.title: Instruction Tuning: Teaching Language Models to Follow Human Intent
item.description:
Large Language Models (LLMs) trained only on raw text are powerful predictors of the next token.
But without further alignment, they often fail to follow user intent or behave helpfully.
Instruction tuning addresses this gap by fine-tuning LLMs on datasets of instructions and demonstrations, making them better at generalizing to unseen tasks.

Core Innovation

  • Instruction–response supervision: Models are trained on pairs of natural language instructions and desired outputs.
  • Generalization to unseen tasks: Exposure to diverse instructions enables models to follow new tasks zero-shot.
  • Human alignment: Shifts models from raw text generation to human-centered assistance.

Architectural Variants

Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)

Fine-tuning a pretrained model directly on (instruction, input, output) triples.

item.title: Large Concept Models (LCMs): A Paradigm Shift Beyond Token-Level Language Modeling
item.description:
Standard LLMs operate at the token level—chunking text into words or subwords and predicting the next token.
But human thought works differently: we think in concepts, flows, and structures, not just discrete units.

Core Innovation

  • Semantic-level reasoning: The Large Concept Model (LCM) handles text at the sentence (concept) level instead of tokens, using the SONAR multilingual and multimodal embedding space as its foundation.
  • Language and modality-agnostic abstraction: Concepts are universal—independent of language and format—enabling the same reasoning pipeline for text or speech across 200 languages.

Architectural Variants

One-Tower Models

A single encoder-decoder stack directly predicts the next sentence representation in the SONAR space.

item.title: About Me
item.description:
I began programming in 2019, just before the COVID-19 pandemic. When lockdowns started in 2020, while many turned to games and entertainment, I found myself drawn to a documentary about Artificial Intelligence — and that moment changed everything. What started as simple curiosity quickly became a lifelong passion.

Since then, I have explored multiple programming languages, including Python, C, C++, and Rust, building a strong foundation in software development. However, what truly excites me is the intersection of Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics — understanding not just how algorithms work, but why they work.

item.title: Why AI Captured My Curiosity — And Why It Should Capture Yours Too
item.description:
It all started in 2019, just before the world went into lockdown. While friends were playing games or scrolling endlessly through social media, I stumbled upon a documentary about Artificial Intelligence. That one hour changed everything. Suddenly, I realized that AI wasn’t just a buzzword — it was a doorway into a world where mathematics, logic, and creativity collide.

My Journey

From that moment, curiosity turned into passion. I started exploring programming with Python, C, and C++, later experimenting with Rust. Each language taught me something new, but what truly fascinated me was the why behind AI — the mathematics, the algorithms, and the reasoning that makes machines intelligent.
